title: Acme Stream churn: which model should build the retention list
subtitle: Three score columns compared on the same 3,000 rows, with a false positive at EUR 25 and a false negative at EUR 90.

verdict.text: Keep `baseline_score` for now. `gbt_v7` is really better on this file by +0.086 ROC-AUC [+0.059, +0.114], but it is trained on `cancellation_reason` and other columns unknown at list time, so retrain it before trusting that. `logreg_v2` is inside the noise.

sections.title: The comparison
sections.intro: Every model scored the same 3,000 rows and every id is unique, so each difference is paired: 2,000 bootstrap resamples, seed 7, with the same rows drawn for all three. ROC-AUC is the primary metric, set before the run.

blocks.text:
**`logreg_v2` is inside the noise on every metric.** Its ROC-AUC difference of +0.011 has the interval [-0.013, +0.034]: the data rule out a gain above 0.034 and a loss above 0.013, and cannot tell it apart from the baseline inside that range.

**`gbt_v7` ranks better and its probabilities are worse.** ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and cost are better than the baseline with the whole interval above zero, while log loss and Brier are worse with the whole interval below zero. See Calibration.

Read the `gbt_v7` numbers with The recommendation in mind. Its gain is real on this file, but `model/features.py` gives it columns that are not known at list time, so this file does not show what it would do in use. [high]

sections.title: Calibration
sections.intro: A score is calibrated when, among rows given 0.3, about 30 in 100 churn. Each bin holds 300 rows, a tenth of the file, and has a Wilson interval on its observed rate.

blocks.text: **`gbt_v7` is miscalibrated: 8 of 10 bins are outside their interval.** Its mean predicted probability is 0.376 against 0.191 observed, so its scores run about twice too high. In the top bin it says 0.888 and 0.503 churn. Its scores cannot be read as probabilities, and only a threshold measured on data works for it until it is recalibrated on held-out data.
`baseline_score` and `logreg_v2` both have 0 of 10 bins outside their interval: mean predicted 0.189 and 0.190 against 0.191 observed.

blocks.text: **The cost of reading `gbt_v7`'s scores as probabilities.** With a break-even probability of 0.217 (25 divided by 115), `gbt_v7` costs EUR 13,872 per 1,000 on this file against EUR 11,797 at the threshold measured on this file. The break-even rule works for `baseline_score` and `logreg_v2` (EUR 14,578 and EUR 14,245) because their probabilities are calibrated. These break-even costs are point values on this file.

**Assumption on the costs.** [guess] The page uses EUR 25 and EUR 90 as given. The brief gets EUR 90 as 30 percent of a EUR 300 margin, but a churner on the list also receives the EUR 25 credit, so the net value of a correct offer is EUR 65. As a sensitivity, EUR 65 moves the break-even probability from 0.217 to 0.278 and shrinks the list. `gbt_v7` still saves money against the baseline, by EUR 1,371 per 1,000 [382, 2,359], but **`baseline_score` no longer clearly beats sending no offers**: EUR 784 per 1,000 [-175, 1,516].

blocks.text:
**`gbt_v7` on `plan = legacy` is the worst slice.** ROC-AUC 0.573 [0.498, 0.649] on 353 rows, with an interval that reaches chance level at 0.5. It is clearly below its own whole-file value, and worse than the baseline there too, by a paired interval of [-0.183, -0.002] that only just excludes zero.

**`baseline_score` on `region = east`** is clearly below its own whole-file value at 0.595 [0.548, 0.646]. Both candidates are better than the baseline in that region: `gbt_v7` by [+0.063, +0.172], `logreg_v2` by [+0.026, +0.125]. That is the only slice of eight where `logreg_v2` beats the baseline.

**Keep `baseline_score` for now and do not move to either candidate.** `gbt_v7` is the only real gain, but it was trained on columns that are unavailable at list time. Retrain it without them and run this comparison again on a clean holdout. `logreg_v2` is inside the noise, so there is nothing to gain by switching to it.

cells.text: [med] If the features are built as of the snapshot

blocks.title: What stops `gbt_v7` being used as it is, and what makes this file unsafe to rely on

items.title: `gbt_v7` trains on `cancellation_reason`, which exists only after a cancellation
items.evidence: The column is in `FEATURES`, the extract joins `cancellations` with no date limit, and `train.py` fits on every column in `FEATURES`. An active subscriber has no such row at list time. [high] How much of the gain it explains cannot be measured from the predictions file. [med]

items.title: `days_since_last_login` can see logins after the snapshot
items.evidence: `last_login_at` is `max(login_ts)` over all logins with no limit at `snapshot_date`, so the feature uses the future for anyone who logged in after the snapshot. [high]
items.fix: Compute the last login up to `snapshot_date`.

items.title: `nps_last` has no as-of date
items.evidence: The extract joins `nps_latest` on the customer only, so a survey answered after the snapshot can reach the model. [high] Its effect on `gbt_v7` was not measured. [guess]
items.fix: Take the latest answer up to `snapshot_date`.

items.title: `predictions.csv` cannot be the committed test split
items.evidence: The file has 3,000 rows, while `test.csv` has 1,000 and `train.csv` 2,400, which together match the brief's 3,400 labelled rows. `model/score.py` writes no `email` column, yet the file has one. [high] If these rows overlap the training rows, every model's numbers here are flattered. [med]
items.fix: Say where the file came from and rescore rows that were not used for training.

items.title: `gbt_v7` is miscalibrated
items.evidence: 8 of 10 bins are outside their interval, and the mean predicted probability is about twice the observed churn rate.
items.fix: Calibrate on held-out data after retraining, or keep to a threshold measured on data.

items.title: `gbt_v7` may not work on the `legacy` plan
items.evidence: ROC-AUC 0.573 [0.498, 0.649] on 353 rows, below the baseline there.
items.fix: Recheck after retraining; if it holds, use the baseline for `legacy`.

blocks.title: What must happen before a model goes to production
items: Rebuild the features as of `snapshot_date`: drop `cancellation_reason`, bound the last login and the NPS answer at the snapshot.
Retrain `gbt_v7`, score rows that were not used for training and belong to customers not in the training set, and run this comparison again.

Agree the false-negative cost with the retention team: EUR 90 as given, or EUR 65 once the credit paid to a correct offer is counted. Until then, if a list must go out, `baseline_score` at 0.201 gives an offer to 37.3% of subscribers (EUR 90), and at 0.279 to 14.8% (EUR 65). Neither meets the team's bar.
If the retrained model is still miscalibrated, calibrate it on held-out data or keep to a measured threshold, chosen on data other than the data it is judged on.
Check the `legacy` plan again and decide whether that plan needs its own treatment.
Run `/data-scientist:ds-dataset` on `train.csv` and `test.csv` to audit leakage, customers repeated across the split and the label window across the cut date.

blocks.text: The brief's estimate of EUR 60,000 a year in staff time is small against the saving at EUR 90: `baseline_score` saves +1.26M a year against sending no offers [+0.59M, +1.98M]. At EUR 65 the same saving is inside the noise, so the case for any list depends on that cost. The yearly figures assume the file's churn rate and the brief's 480,000 decisions. [guess]

items: How much of `gbt_v7`'s gain comes from the leaking columns. That needs a retrained model, not this file.

Whether the 3,000 rows overlap the training rows, or whether a customer appears on both sides of the split. `/data-scientist:ds-dataset` is the audit for this. Only the header line and line count of `train.csv` and `test.csv` were read, no rows.

Whether a model finds the subscribers an offer would keep. The label is churn and the file does not say who already received an offer, so a model can rank likely churners without ranking those an offer would save. The brief's 30 percent save rate is taken as it stands.
Time and drift: the intervals cover sampling noise only, on one holdout.
The brief's login-count rule, reported there as about 4 in 10 right and 1 in 5 found. The predictions file has no login count, so it was not compared here.
Model training details, serving, and the EUR 60,000 staff estimate.
The file holds a personal column, `email`, that was neither used nor printed. Nothing here needs it, so drop it from the file.

blocks.title: Assumptions
items: [guess] Assumption: the costs are EUR 25 and EUR 90 as given, with a true positive costing nothing. EUR 65 is run as a sensitivity because a correct offer still pays the EUR 25 credit.
[guess] Assumption: ROC-AUC is the primary metric, chosen before the run, and the decision itself rests on out-of-sample cost.
[guess] Assumption: `predictions.csv` is treated as the holdout, as the README calls it, although its size does not match `test.csv`.
[guess] Assumption: `baseline_score` is the score in use today, from the README's "the current score", and it and `logreg_v2` do not use the leaking columns. Their training code is not in the repo.
[guess] Assumption: one row is one independent decision. The file has no customer id, so a customer in several snapshots would make the intervals too narrow.
[guess] Assumption: the team's bar means recall of at least 33.3% and precision of at least 40% at one threshold, from "one in three" and "no more than 6 in 10 wasted".
[guess] Assumption: yearly figures use the brief's 480,000 decisions and the file's 19.1% churn rate, which is above the brief's 16 to 17 in 100.
